messages.subject: Comparing non-nested models
parts:
Hello all, 

I am confused whether these two non-nested models can be compared using the AIC outputted by lavaan. If not, is there any other way to compare the models?

model1 <- 
'Int =~ item1 + item2 + item3 + item4 + item5 
Ext =~ item6 + item7 + item8 + item9 + item10
p =~  item1 + item2 + item3 + item4 + item5 +  item6 + item7 + item8 + item9 + item10 

Outcome2 ~ p + Outcome1 + control1 + control2 + Int + Ext
Outcome1 ~ p + control1 + control2 + Int + Ext'

model2 <- 
'Int1 =~ item1 + item2 + item3 + item4 + item5 
Ext1 =~ item6 + item7 + item8 + item9 + item10
WB =~ item 11 + item12 + item13 + item14 + item15 + item16 + item17
c =~  item1 + item2 + item3 + item4 + item5 +  item6 + item7 + item8 + item9 + item10 + item 11 + item12 + item13 + item14 + item15 + item16 + item17 

Outcome2 ~ c + Outcome1 + control1 + control2 + Int1 + Ext1 + WB
Outcome1 ~ c + control1 + control2 + Int1 + Ext1 + WB'

Thank you 

Warm regards, 
Ritika

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Comparing non-nested models
parts: I understand that the limitation of this approach is that I am treating the factor scores as observed variables, meaning that measurement error is not taken into account

No, factor scores are expected to be free of measurement error.  But treating them as observations does not account for sampling error.

Factor indeterminacy is also an issue.
is it possible to compare these two mediation models with same endogenous, but different exogenous variables?

No, because one set of exogenous predictors is not a subset of the other.  Both of these are nested in a more general model that includes all predictors:

Outcome2 ~ p + c + Outcome1 + control1 + control2 + Int + Ext + Int1 + Ext1 + WB
Outcome1 ~ p + c +            control1 + control2 + Int + Ext + Int1 + Ext1 + WB

Each of your 2 models set some of these coefficients to 0.  What you could do is use Vuong's LRT for nonnested model comparison.  Doing so would require fitting a model that includes all variables, but sets some coefficients to zero.  For example, your med_model1 is

Outcome2 ~ p + 0*c + Outcome1 + control1 + control2 + Int + Ext + 0*Int1 + 0*Ext1 + 0*WB
Outcome1 ~ p + 0*c +            control1 + control2 + Int + Ext + 0*Int1 + 0*Ext1 + 0*WB

Vuong's test is available in the nonnest2 package.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

parts:
From: lav...@googlegroups.com <lav...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com>
Date: Thursday, 11. January 2024 at 13.53
To: lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: Re: Comparing non-nested models
I understand that the limitation of this approach is that I am treating the factor scores as observed variables, meaning that measurement error is not taken into account
No, factor scores are expected to be free of measurement error.  But treating them as observations does not account for sampling error.

Factor scores are calculated as weighted sums of indicators that are contaminated with measurement error. Therefore, factor scores are not “free of measurement error”.

 

 

The fundamental issue that you are facing is that the model comparison statistics that you are using are designed to estimate how well two different models approximate the same covariance matrix. You are trying to use two different models to approximate two different covariance matrices. If the models differ in terms of model fit, would you blame the model differences or the covariance differences?  It is difficult to see what research question such comparison would be useful for.

 

Mikko
